awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation potential of a microbial-based, multi-target biopesticide for crop protection and pest management
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of sustainable, multi-target biopesticides that address major pest management challenges and crop losses for U.S. farmers. Pests are responsible for a 20-40% annual reduction in crop yields in the U.S., posing a serious threat to agricultural productivity. Traditional chemical pesticides, which dominate over 90% of the U.S. pesticide market, have resulted in widespread resistance, significantly diminishing their effectiveness. Additionally, 99% of these pesticides are derived from petroleum, contributing to environmental degradation and water contamination in over 50% of U.S. agricultural regions. This project aims to replace these harmful chemicals with efficacious, cost-effective, and customizable biopesticides. These biopesticides have the potential to reduce pesticide costs by 40%, particularly for high-value crops like almonds and citrus, while providing a safer and more sustainable alternative. Designed to supplement the existing pest management toolkit, these agro-biologicals may enhance integrated pest control management, focusing on delaying resistance onset and selectively targeting pests while preserving beneficial pollinators and biodiversity.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of microbial-based, multi-target biopesticides using synthetic biology techniques. The proposed technology enables the efficient and versatile integration of large DNA segments from one microbe to another, allowing for the merging of entire pesticidal operons and genetic pathways sourced from diverse microorganisms in nature. To address concerns about unwanted environmental spread of microbes and health risks associated with genetically modified organisms, these engineered microbes are transformed into non-reproducing, biodegradable particles that mimic commercial spore products. This approach ensures environmental safety while preserving pesticidal effectiveness.  In addition, engineering efforts are reduced while expanding the range of possibilities for pest control solutions.  Preliminary results have shown the successful integration of pesticidal traits, significantly enhancing efficacy against microbial pests compared to traditional chemical standards. The proposed technology offers broad-spectrum pest control and extends the product's effective application cycles, and is designed to integrate seamlessly with existing pesticide systems.  This technology may deliver a sustainable, long-term solution to current pest management challenges by addressing resistance and improving crop protection.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Insect pests, weeds, and plant diseases destroy a large share of the food grown in the United States each year, by some estimates 20 to 40 percent of potential crop yields. Farmers fight back mostly with chemical pesticides, but these chemicals are losing their effectiveness as pests develop resistance, and the vast majority are made from petroleum, raising cost and environmental concerns. This project explored the commercial potential of a new kind of crop protection product designed to address both problems at once.

The underlying technology uses synthetic biology to combine several natural pest-fighting compounds, drawn from different microbes found in nature, into a single product. Rather than releasing live genetically modified organisms into fields, which raises safety and environmental concerns, the engineered microbes are turned into non-reproducing, biodegradable particles. The particles carry the active compounds but can't grow or spread on their own. Combining several modes of action in a single product is meant to control more kinds of pests at once, slow down resistance, and leave pollinators like bees alone.

The purpose of this NSF I-Corps award was not to conduct laboratory research but to test whether a real market exists for this technology. Over the course of the project, the team interviewed a wide range of stakeholders across the agricultural system: farm owners and managers, growers of different crops, agricultural retailers and distributors, and the pest control advisors who guide purchasing decisions. The team began with California growers and, as early assumptions proved wrong, expanded to larger farms, cooperatives, and citrus growers in other regions. 

The interviews reshaped the team's understanding of the opportunity in several important ways. The first assumption was that small organic farms, the sustainability-minded ones, would be the earliest customers. That was wrong. Small growers tend to stick with cheap, hands-off methods and rarely buy specialized pest products at all. The better fit turned out to be larger farms and cooperatives, which lose more money when pests hit and are more willing to pay for something that works. Almost everyone the team talked to came back to the same two points: it has to work, and it has to be affordable. Being green was nice but never enough by itself to close a sale. One grower put it bluntly: if it doesn't work, it doesn't matter how green it is.

The team also learned that pest problems don't look the same from one place to the next. They shift with climate, geography, and crop, which killed the idea of one broad, national market. And farmers, it turned out, almost never buy directly from the people who develop a technology. They buy through distributors and trusted advisors. Any real product would have to reach them through those channels.

Through these conversations, the team identified a specific high-need opportunity: citrus groves in Florida, Texas, and Mexico devastated by Citrus Greening disease, a destructive infection with few effective treatments. This kind of focused, urgent problem represents the type of market where a new biological solution could deliver meaningful value. 

Weighing all of this, the team decided not to push this particular technology further right now. Deciding that on the basis of evidence, instead of chasing an idea customers didn't want, is one of the main things I-Corps is designed to teach.

The broader impacts of the work extend beyond the specific technology. It trained working scientists in customer research, market analysis, and stakeholder engagement, which is useful whether they end up in industry, startups, or technology transfer. It also produced a clearer, evidence-based picture of how agricultural innovations actually reach farmers, and that picture should help future researchers build with those realities in mind from the start.
